c.tagline: The largest city of Western Sahara, on the edge of the Atlantic Sahara.

taxi.fareNote: Small 'petits taxis' work within the city and are cheap and metered — insist on the meter (compteur) or agree a price first, and expect to share the cab with other riders. Larger white 'grands taxis' cover the airport and longer runs at a negotiated flat rate. There are no ride-hailing apps.

emergency.note: Dial 19 for police and 15 for ambulance/fire; 112 also works from mobiles. French and Arabic are the languages of officialdom.

solo.f: comfortable if dressed modestly; extra caution

hood_landmark.Foum el Oued: Foum el Oued beach Laayoune Morocco

avoid.reason: No specific no-go districts in town, but stay away from political demonstrations and never travel off-road toward the sand berm east of the territory, which is mined.
Photographing police, military or government buildings can draw questioning in this heavily policed disputed territory; petty crime is otherwise low.

hood_desc: The old Spanish-built colonial quarter at the city's heart, with the whitewashed former cathedral of San Francisco de Asis, the grand Place du Mechouar square and the main administrative buildings; the most walkable base for a first visit.
A central residential and commercial district with markets, cafes and mid-range hotels, giving an everyday feel of the city away from the monumental core.
A large, densely built residential district that grew from earlier tent and self-built housing; local and unpolished, with basic shops and little tourism.
A newer administrative and residential area of wide avenues, government offices and modern apartment blocks; quieter and more spread out.

The Atlantic beach suburb roughly 20 km west at the mouth of the Saguia el-Hamra, with a long sandy shoreline, seaside residences, the fishing port and the city's beach hotels; a weekend escape from the desert heat.

water.note: Stick to bottled water in this desert city.

transit.pay: Pay the bus fare in cash to the driver (a few dirhams); petits taxis are metered and cheap. There is no rechargeable transit card.
transit.hours: City buses run roughly from early morning to mid-evening; petits taxis fill the gaps day and night.
transit.note: Laayoune has no metro, tram or rail; getting around means a basic municipal bus network and, above all, the cheap metered petits taxis for hops around town, with grands taxis for the airport and longer desert runs.

tip.r: ~5-10% at sit-down restaurants for good service; round up taxi fares and leave a few dirhams for cafe and hotel staff.

landmarks: Moulay Abdel Aziz Grand Mosque
The city's principal mosque, its slender minaret rising above whitewashed ochre facades as the spiritual centerpiece of Laayoune's modern quarter.
Spanish Cathedral (St. Francis of Assisi)
A striking 1950s modernist church with twin domed towers, a rare surviving emblem of the Spanish colonial era in the old town.
Place du Mechouar (Oum Saad Square)
Laayoune's vast ceremonial plaza framed by arcades and towers, the stage for national celebrations and evening strolls in the desert cool.
Colline aux Oiseaux
A walled garden aviary and small zoo in the city center where peacocks, parrots and desert plants offer shady respite from Saharan heat.
Saguia el-Hamra Riverbed
The wide, usually dry 'Red Canal' wadi spanned by the city's bridges, its palm-dotted banks and dunes marking Laayoune's dramatic desert setting.
Old Spanish Quarter (Colonial Lower Town)
The original 1930s Spanish settlement of domed cubist houses and military buildings clustered near the wadi, an atmospheric slice of colonial Sahara.
Souk Djemal (camel market district)
Laayoune's earthy market quarter where Sahrawi traders deal in camels, dates and desert provisions, offering an authentic window on nomadic commerce.
Ensemble Artisanal (craft complex)
A government craft center where Sahrawi artisans work silver jewelry, leather and indigo textiles, the best place to watch and buy authentic handicrafts.
Foum el Oued Beach
Laayoune's seaside escape twenty kilometers west, where the Saguia el-Hamra meets a wild Atlantic shore of dunes, surf and weekend villas.
Souk ez-Zaj
A small covered market for local spices, dried dates, crafts and traditional fabrics, distinct from Laayoune's larger camel-trading souk.

train.note: There is no railway in Western Sahara. Morocco's ONCF network reaches only as far south as Marrakech, roughly 1,100 km north of Laayoune, and although an extension towards Agadir and the south has been studied for years, no track has been laid. All surface travel is by coach, shared taxi or private vehicle along the N1 coastal highway.

intl.to: Agadir, Marrakech, Tan-Tan & Dakhla (Morocco & Western Sahara)
intl.op: Supratours (ONCF's coach arm) — tickets at the Laayoune bus station

bus.note: Coaches use the gare routière on the edge of Laayoune, where CTM and Supratours both have ticket offices alongside the cheaper local companies; Supratours fares can be combined with an ONCF train ticket from Marrakech. Agadir is around 10-11 hours, Marrakech 16-18 hours and Dakhla 8-9 hours south, mostly overnight, and buses are modern but the road has frequent police checkpoints where you hand over your passport details, so carry photocopies of a printed 'fiche'. Note that Western Sahara is administered by Morocco and services are marketed as domestic Moroccan routes. For onward travel to Mauritania you continue to Dakhla and then take a shared 4x4 or minibus to the Guerguerat border post; there is no scheduled through coach from Laayoune to Nouadhibou or Nouakchott.

ferry.note: Laayoune's harbour at El Marsa, about 25 km from the city, is a phosphate and fishing port with no passenger services, and the former ferry between Tarfaya and Fuerteventura in the Canary Islands has not operated for years, so there is currently no sea link from this stretch of coast.

half.name: Foum el Oued & Laayoune Plage
half.blurb: The city's Atlantic beach at the mouth of the Saguia el-Hamra, about 20-25 km west, with a long sandy shore, seaside cafes and the fishing port of Laayoune-Plage.

half.name: Saguia el-Hamra desert fringe
half.blurb: The seasonal riverbed and palm-dotted desert edge just outside the city, a taste of the surrounding Sahara and dromedary country.

full.name: Khenifiss National Park
full.blurb: North along the coast, the Naila Lagoon shelters flamingos and migratory birds amid dunes and salt flats in the Sahara's finest coastal wetland.
